*Update* {{2025-12-02}}

* Braze calculation of deliverability: (sent - bounce) / sent. However this number is far off from what we have in our data as discussed here [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09HMUJEUSW/p1764157763667959|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09HMUJEUSW/p1764157763667959|smart-link]
* @ / Dovainis Kaleda reached out to Braze and according to Braze, bounce is only calculated for hard bounce and soft bounce is still considered as delivered. Therefore the deliverability calculation should be: (sent - (email delivered + soft bounce)) / sent
* This suggested calculation from Braze, however, still leaves 2% gap in the data which, according to Braze, stems from timezone offset (UTC vs local time).

We had our first sync with Docebo onboarding manager today. 

Next steps: 

Course completion data migration - we need to put together a file that will be uploaded to Docebo 

Learning Plan completion - course completion migration can only be done on a course level, so even if all the courses are marked as completed within the learning plan, it will not automatically make the learning plan complete. Docebo will have to figure out what would be the best option for us, as they could complete the learning plan for us.

Data migration (user data) - this part is done by IT, once it is completed, we can set up enrollment automation



Some dates to remember: 

The pilot finishes on 19 December, so if there are no issues from IH, the entire IH should / can move to Docebo on 22 December. Of course this can be done after the Christmas holidays, depending on your availability. New BPO to be onboarded somewhere in January, so everything to be ready for them. Other BPOs also to transition in January 2026, but you can create a transition plan.


Example: Move Mplus first on 05 January (again, depending on your schedule), then Transcom on 19 January etc etc.--> Platform to be ready for new BPO by January 2026. Since there is no exact date for their onboarding yet, play it safe and have everything ready by 05/01.

Data migration: Has to be done before you can implement enrolment automations. If not possible (due to Okta delay or other reasons), you can still onboard BPOs, just keep the old workflow of requesting enrolment for Onboarding via SD.


Expected deadline for IT to finish Okta integration is 5 December.

Hi [~accountid:712020:fde8e40a-0c43-479b-a07d-dd05334dd10a] it is valid, but sometimes the other party required qualified electronic signature or wet ink. 

FYI for future requests, please note that according to the Transaction Approval and Signatory Policy, legal approval is *not required* for spend contracts *below EUR 5,000*, unless one of the specific “Legal Approval Requirements” in Annex 1 applies (e.g., privacy terms, exclusivity, Infosec, penalties on Bolt, etc.). Where legal approval is not required, *Legal does not sign* these agreements. For details please see this page or ask Flank at [https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C09HVLVM0KH|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C09HVLVM0KH|smart-link] (SK) or [https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C095J7BT64Q|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C095J7BT64Q|smart-link] (CZ)

If no legal approval is required, you can submit directly to Legal Ops for signing, it will significantly speed up the process. In case of doubts which ticket should be submitted, you can always ask Flank.

Thank you!

we look at materiality from two perspectives:

*financial perspective* -

* external auditors do procedures to check if our numbers are reliable / properly calculated
* immaterial - determine which accounts are relevant, which are not. Not relevant is immaterial.
* material - has relevant & significant effect on the financial statement, *which should be recorded, but is not (so this is related to whether information is correct)*. this is material.
* 5% of revenue/EBITDA. this is a strict number. FULLY NUMBERS

*risk perspective* -

* if there is a risk that is below materiality threshold, then nothing is done.
* if there is a risk that is above threshold, then It will be escalated because it’s significant business risk.
* materiality from risk perspective doesn’t have to be strict number, e.g 5% of revenue/EBIDTA, but you can also have *fines*, *license* *loss, negative exposure in media* etc, it might not have an impact only on the financial statement.

Internal Audit highlighted we should aim to categorise them further as follows:

* group level
* country level (we can consider to also cluster them, e.g. Nigeria and Kenya together)
* vertical level

We should define financial/accounting and risk perspective materiality together:

* define company’s/management’s risk appetite
** they can have different dimensions, vertical based
* define risk perspective thresholds based on the risk appetite
* define financial/accounting perspective thresholds based on the risk appetite

*02.12.2025: Feedback from Consumer protection Office (Estonian POC for DSA related questions:*

*_Transparency reports do not need to be submitted to the transparency database; only the decisions and reasons referred to in_* [*_Article 17_*|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj?locale=et#d1e2543-1-1] *_of the DSA need to be submitted_* _(Article 24(5) of the DSA). These must be submitted without undue delay immediately after the restriction has been imposed (Article 66 of the DSA). Therefore, if you have not yet made a restrictive decision referred to in Article 17 in relation to any service recipient, you do not yet need to submit anything to the transparency database._

_All the information about the data schema of the DSA Transparency Database is available on the_ [_database website_|https://transparency.dsa.ec.europa.eu/page/documentation]_. The Helpdesk team is available for any techncal questions platforms might have about submissions:_ [CNECT-DSA-HELPDESK@ec.europa.eu|mailto:CNECT-DSA-HELPDESK@ec.europa.eu]

_The choice of whether to use the API or the web form to submit your reasons is yours. Regarding the question of how to make a choice about the way to send submissions to the Transparency Database to the European Commission, whether via: web form vs. API (sending justifications separately) vs. API (sending justifications "in bulk"): This is really up to each platform, depending on their needs. Typically, platforms with a high volume of submissions choose the API while platforms with a lower submission volume choose the webform._

 _Transparency reports however do not need to be submitted to the Commission, but need to be published by the platforms themselves in the format specified in the implementing regulation. More information about the technical functioning of the API can be found_ [_HERE_|https://transparency.dsa.ec.europa.eu/page/api-documentation?lang=et] _and about the web form_ [_HERE_|https://transparency.dsa.ec.europa.eu/page/webform-documentation?lang=et]_._

_To join the transparency database, please first fill out_ [_THIS_|https://ec.europa.eu/eusurvey/runner/DSA-ComplianceStamentsReasons#page0] _form. After that, we can continue with the registration of your database in our systems. This is the first time we have added a platform to the transparency database, so we will learn how to do it together with you._

*GRC NOTES on Materiality:*

*Materiality Threshold for Reporting* 

The need for a *materiality matrix* has been identified to distinguish between Group-level and subsidiary-level reporting thresholds. The purpose of today’s introductory discussion is to: 

* Introduce the concept of a materiality threshold 
* Discuss why it is required and its strategic importance
* Agree / disagree to implement and align on next steps 

*What do we mean by a materiality threshold for reporting?* 

* *Materiality* - is a key accounting principle that determines whether a discrepancy, such as an omission or misstatement, would impact a reasonable user’s decision-making. If it would, the information is material. If the information is insignificant or irrelevant, it is said to be immaterial. 
* *Group level materiality* - refers to the threshold of what is reported for the purposes of the consolidated financial statements.
* In principle, the Group-level materiality should be higher, while subsidiaries operate with lower thresholds. 
* The internal materiality threshold should be set slightly lower than that used by external auditors to enable more proactive internal oversight. A two-tier approach could be adopted:
** A lower materiality level for noting and tracking issues.
** A higher materiality level for deciding when an issue requires addressing.



*Why is this required?* 

* Demonstrates compliance with accounting principles. 
* Demonstrates that our financial statements are prepared fairly. 
* This framework will also influence issue prioritisation, with Group-level matters addressed with higher urgency.



If the GRC Committee agrees that the threshold is required, the Global Risk & Compliance Team will work with the Finance / Internal Audit Team to prepare a proposal for the GRC Committee to confirm the acceptable materiality level (€m) and establish a clear framework for determining the scale of issues that need to be addressed by Bolt. 



Below is an initial proposal for the GRC Committee to use as a starting point for today’s discussion:

Materiality from Risk perspective should be lower or same as the risk appetite. Need to define a threshold for risk appetite

Materiality for Accounting focuses more on the accuracy of financial statements for reporting and auditing purposes.

Thresholds from a Financial perspective & thresholds from Risk Management (could be defined from financial statements AND from qualitative risks), and thresholds for the company’s and management’s Risk Appetite levels

We look at materiality from two perspectives:

*financial perspective* -

* external auditors do procedures to check if our numbers are reliable / properly calculated
* immaterial - determine which accounts are relevant, which are not. Not relevant is immaterial.
* material - has relevant & significant effect on the financial statement, *which should be recorded, but is not (so this is related to whether information is correct)*. this is material.
* 5% of revenue/EBITDA. this is a strict number. FULLY NUMBERS

*risk perspective* -

* if there is a risk that is below materiality threshold, then nothing is done.
* if there is a risk that is above threshold, then It will be escalated because it’s significant business risk.
* materiality from risk perspective doesn’t have to be strict number, e.g 5% of revenue/EBIDTA, but you can also have *fines*, *license* *loss, negative exposure in media* etc, it might not have an impact on the financial statement.

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

Hey,

In France we have commission netting.

_Through commission netting, your campaigns/bonuses/compensations are reflected as a discount from your commission, instead of each having their individual invoices. Simply, your commission is reduced in the amount of your campaigns/bonuses/compensations - ensuring a more clear invoicing process, and less invoicing noise._

_For example, previously you would see a commission of 416.91€ and separate bonus lines of 11€ on your invoice, which totaled up to 361.92€. Now, you would only see a single row of commission in the amount of 361.92€, meaning the calculation is already done in the background._



Example for some [Driver|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet/drivers/edit/3318350?tab=profile&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn]:

Taking November 2025 example from [Balance history|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/balanceHistory?balanceHistoryFilterSearch=%7B%22external_id%22%3A3318350%2C%22type%22%3A%22Driver%22%2C%22month%22%3A%7B%22month%22%3A11%2C%22year%22%3A2025%7D%2C%22viewType%22%3A%22monthly%22%2C%22week%22%3A%7B%22start%22%3A1762725600000%2C%22end%22%3A1763330399999%7D%7D]. 

Commission that driver had to pay is

{quote}*Commission = expense_cash_commission* + *expense_commission* (48.50 EUR + 190.83 EUR) = €239.33 EUR{quote}

this commission is ±20% of the amount driver had in Ride fees

{quote}Fees = *earning_in_app_ride_fee* + *earning_cash_ride_fee* (947.70 EUR + 242.50 EUR) = €1,190.20 EUR

Commission % = commission / fees = €239.33 EUR / 1,190.20 EUR = 0.20 = 20%{quote}

the [invoice|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-document/invoices/5649895597?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] was issued for 132.94 euro, which is less than 239.33 because we do *commission netting* in Estonia.

{quote}*What is Commission Netting?*

*Commission netting* is a process used to simplify how drivers are invoiced for commissions, especially when there are bonuses, campaigns, or compensations involved.

*Without Netting:*

Normally, a driver would receive separate invoices:

One for the commission they owe (e.g., 20% of ride fees)

Separate invoices for any bonuses, campaigns, or compensations they receive

*With Netting (as done in Estonia):*

Instead of issuing multiple invoices, the system *reduces the commission amount* by the total value of any bonuses, campaigns, or compensations the driver earned.

The driver receives a *single, lower commission invoice* that already accounts for these discounts.{quote}

You can see discounts earned via cash and app rides in *earning_cash_discount_netted* and *earning_in_app_discount_netted.*

So we can calculate the final netted commission like this:

{quote}Netted Commission = Commission - *earning_cash_discount_netted - earning_in_app_discount_netted* = €239.33 - 26.70 EUR - 79.70 EUR = €132.93{quote}

132.93 is the same amount you can see on Monthly invoice (take invoice from November from [+here+|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients/128179276?tab=partner_invoices&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn])

✨ That’s how you can calculate Commission Netting in Balance history.

Nikolay Roll

h3. What {{deregistration_delay}} actually does (quick recap)

For ALB/NLB target groups, {{deregistration_delay}} is the time the load balancer *waits before forcibly closing existing connections* after a target has been marked for removal:

* During the delay:
** No *new* requests are sent to the target.
** Existing connections/requests can keep going.
* When the delay expires:
** Any remaining connections are *closed* by the load balancer.

So it’s a “drain time” for in-flight requests during:

* Auto Scaling scale-in
* Instance/container shutdown
* Deployments where targets are deregistered from the group
* Manual deregistration




h3. Risks of setting it very low

h4. 1. In-flight requests get cut off mid-way

If your typical request duration is longer than the delay, you will periodically:

* Drop client connections mid-request.
* Cause users to see errors

Hey [~accountid:63f5ed783ec8aa51d3d2a025], 

Key issues that pose significant risk for Bolt if we sign this tender:

* *Unlimited contractual liability for Bolt*, meaning that if any issues arise, Bolt would be obliged to compensate _all_ losses incurred by the Contracting Authority; in addition, there are contractual penalties (up to €1,000 per incident for service issues and €2,000 per confidentiality breach), while the Contracting Authority would still retain the right to claim additional damages.
* *Definitions and how Bolt is framed in the tender*: the wording suggests that Bolt itself provides the food delivery services and that the delivery partners are Bolt’s employees, for whose improper conduct Bolt is directly liable. This contradicts Bolt’s business model and may look very problematic in the context of the PWD and potential reclassification.
* *The agreement is valid for 24 months, with the possibility to extend it for another 24 months at the discretion of the institution.* Under clause 10.2 it is not clear whether this is entirely a unilateral decision of the institution, which could lead to disagreements and disputes.
* *Bolt has no right to unilaterally terminate the contract*, unless such a right is provided for by law. In substance, this means there are no realistic options for Bolt to exit the agreement, unless the institution commits a material breach.

These are only the main and most significant risks; there are additional ones as well, which should be assessed by the Privacy team and etc.

Hi [~accountid:712020:3db0aede-64e8-4fb8-ba39-3f2a1189572b] 

Bolt Balance can be rolled out in Paraguay, but *only without the Top Up feature*. In practice, this means customers must not be able to load funds into Bolt Balance directly from their card or bank account. This is because allowing customer funded top ups could likely be qualified as *issuing a prepaid payment instrument* under certain countries financial regulation, which in turn could trigger licensing and other regulatory requirements (which we do not have). So to avoid any regulatory exposure, Bolt Balance in Paraguay should be funded only through Bolt-originated transactions (e.g. compensations, incentives).

Bolt Balance in PY should only work for: 

* Reflecting debt from customers (failed payments, etc.)
* Making funds available as compensation (customer complains about the services and receives X amount a gesture of good will from CS).

As per the UK, rating thresholds can appear like_ *_performance management_*_, suggesting Bolt is supervising or directing drivers, which undermines the independence required for an agency-based contractor model. The risk in Ireland is assessed as_ *_🟠 Medium_* _given the absence of claims but the potential for such a feature to be used as evidence of control if challenged in future._

_As with the UK, to mitigate this, the feature should be kept_ *_purely informational_*_, with_ *_no minimum rating_* _and_ *_no link_* _to allocation, earnings or rewards. A safer approach is to base “Top Driver” on_ *_general, non-numeric positive rider feedback_* _rather than any score or threshold. With these adjustments, the risk can be reduced to_ *_🟢 Low_* _for the Irish market._

A mandatory *automated* selfie-check requires processing of _biometric data_ (unique face features) for the purpose of identity verification. Under the GDPR, biometric data used to uniquely identify a person is a +special category of personal data+ and its use requires:

* a clear lawful basis under Art. 6 (likely _legitimate interest_ or _legal obligation_), *and*
* a valid Art. 9 derogation (e.g., likely _substantial public interest_ established by law).

Without explicit statutory support, the proposed measure is unlikely to meet these conditions. We may rely on user’s explicit consent before processing their biometric data; however, this approach implies that users may disagree and request manual process discussed below.

Alternative approach is to have *manual* selfie-check performed by a human agent before each order. But this option is operationally slow, costly, intrusive, and difficult to scale. It introduces significant latency and privacy risks (misuse or accidental disclosure). I believe these risks should also be explained to the authority.

Hey, the issue is not because of duplicate source file {{bolt_dbt}} should not have any effect on this since your project doesn't depend on this.

The main problem seems to be in the staging model.

To give context

* Staging is a view model.
* View is created in CI/CD step after merge ([reference|https://github.com/bolteu/dbt/actions/runs/19858396800/job/56902713126] for your merged PR [@dmitry.zamaleev|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/UN8C7ULLX])
* View creation depends whether there's any changes in the view files itself.

*What does this mean?*

The updated source require you to also make some "dummy" update to the staging files. Our CI/CD doesn't detect any changes to the {{.sql}} file of the staging and hence it doesn't recreate the view representation with the new source.

On your dev however, if you use {{dbt build -s +your_model}} this will refresh everything including your staging model in you dev, hence everything will be updated.

*How to fix this?*

You can refresh your staging definition that depends on the new source through a Github Action. You can follow the tutorial [*here*|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/DATA/pages/5093490790/Working+with+view+models#Avoiding-stale-view] (see avoiding stale view). (edited) 

[*Working with view models*|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/DATA/pages/5093490790/Working+with+view+models?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiYmZhM2M3ODlmZDQ0NGU2M2IwM2I1OTE0NTU1ZWYwNmMiLCJwIjoiY29uZmx1ZW5jZS1jaGF0cy1pbnQifQ]

I now have [recreated the view|https://github.com/bolteu/dbt/actions/runs/19888113212/job/56999951560] & [triggered the backfill|https://bolt-common.cloud.databricks.com/jobs/1063840428959247/runs/377096297781554?o=3598988355446810] again. I'll try to help check if this is solving the problem or not (edited)

* Bolt LT should declare the taxable income monthly declarations in the *GPM313* form (by 15th of the same month – when prizes, gifts or winnings are paid out by the 15th of that month; OR until the last day of the same month, when prizes, gifts or winnings are paid out after the 15th day of that month) and annual declarations in the *GPM312* form. Hey [~accountid:712020:60da7793-200e-4a92-a78d-1705c6e5cdf8], thanks for the update! 
I think this kind of combination is _in principle_ possible under LT law, but only as a promotional prize campaign, *not* a “lottery” under the Lottery Law, and with clearer wording than you currently have.

# *Combined mechanic (top 3 + random from 300+ rides)*
Legally you can run one campaign with two “prize buckets”:
#* *non-random* prizes (top 3 based on a clearly pre-defined metric), and
#* *random* prizes (drawn among all drivers who completed 300+ trips).
As long as participation is linked only to providing services on the platform (driving) and not to buying “tickets” or paying a separate participation fee, it should not qualify as a licensed lottery under the Lottery Law.
# *Do* *_not_* *use the word “lottery” in external comms*
The moment you call it a “lottery”, the regulator gets an easy hook to ask whether this falls under the Lottery Law (licence, tax, etc.). Externally, call it a “prize game” / “campaign”, and in the rules clearly explain that prizes are awarded (i) to the top 3 by X metric, and (ii) randomly to 47 others from the 300+ group.
# *Do we need to specify exact prizes or is “small technical items/vouchers” enough?*
Unfair commercial practices / advertising rules require that the information about prizes is not misleading and does not hide key characteristics (type, value).
#* “Small technical items” is too vague – a driver might expect €100 headphones and get a €10 power bank.
#* Safer wording: “partner vouchers (e.g. car wash, spare parts) worth approx. €XX and technical accessories (e.g. headphones, power banks) worth approx. €XX.”
The law doesn’t force you to state an exact model, but you should define the type and value level clearly enough.
# *Do we need to specify the exact number of winners?*
There’s no literal provision saying “you must state the number of winners”, but the number of prizes and the allocation rules are material information – hiding them can be seen as a misleading omission.
My suggestion:
#* in the rules, clearly state: “there will be 50 winners in total: 3 top drivers and 47 randomly selected from drivers who completed ≥300 trips”;
#* if you want flexibility, you can say “up to 50 winners”, but then you cannot arbitrarily award significantly fewer prizes than you advertised.
# *Two points I suggest fixing before launch*
#* The term “guaranteed prizes game”: don’t use it unless _every_ driver actually receives something. Otherwise, you’re inviting a misleading-practice argument (you promise “guaranteed”, but only a fraction get anything).
#* “Top 3 drivers” must have a crystal-clear metric: by what? number of trips, revenue, rating, a combination? The rules must spell this out so there’s no room for manual tweaking or discrimination claims later.

If you have any additional questions, please let me know, thanks!

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


The refund is successfully completed. I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

h3. +*Draft response to the business:*+

Hi [~accountid:62ff8d58b582d07a14a96588],

We’ve now reviewed the proposal, and from a legal and privacy perspective you *can move forward* with using Prezzee, *subject to the steps below*. For ease of reference and completeness, I’ve copied and summarised [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a]’s privacy comments directly into this message so you have everything in one place.

# +*Worker Status / Reclassification risk*+

Providing vouchers linked to performance indicators (e.g. high trip volume, GMV, online hours) can theoretically be treated as an employment-type benefit. The risk here is *low*, as the value is small, infrequent, and framed as appreciation — but please ensure the following mitigations are applied:

* Treat the vouchers as *one-off goodwill gestures*, not earned rewards.
* Avoid wording such as *“bonus”, “reward”, “performance”, “compensation”*, or anything implying entitlement.
* Issue the communication via *marketing/comms*, not payments or operations.
* Keep monetary value low and occasional.
* Include a brief disclaimer making clear the voucher is *not consideration for services and is not part of driver earnings*.

Thank you for raising this ticket.

Our [*General T&Cs for Service Providers* |https://bolt.eu/en-mt/legal/tnc-service-provider/?category=rides]*state the following:*

* A Driver’s right to access any Category exists _“only for so long as the Driver meets the applicable Category requirements”_ (3.4.4).
* Section 5.20–5.21 confirms that:
- Bolt decides which Categories exist in a market; and
- The Categories available to a Driver depend on factors relevant to each Category and the marketplace, and a Driver’s right to access _“will lapse if the Driver no longer meets the requirements for that Category”._
* Bolt can restrict access to protect integrity / reputation:
- Access rights exist only “for such periods that use of the Bolt Platform would not cause significant harm to its integrity or reputation”.
- Bolt may also suspend or restrict access where needed to prevent “other significant harm to the integrity or reputation of the Bolt Platform”.
* P2B / complaint handling is covered: if Bolt takes a decision the Service Provider disagrees with (including Category access), they can submit a complaint or request a review under the internal complaint-handling rules (section 16.8).

So, contractually, if a car with premium characteristics no longer meets the Category requirements (e.g. “no visible damage / premium exterior”), Bolt is expressly entitled to withdraw access to that Category.
This is exactly what results from 3.4.4 + 5.20–5.21.
The car still being _roadworthy_ doesn’t change that, since this is about meeting the marketplace’s own quality requirements for higher-priced Categories.

*On the Maltese regulatory framework:*

Under S.L. 499.68 (Light Passenger Transport Services and Vehicle Hire Services Regulations), Operators must ensure vehicles used for hire are _“clean, well maintained and in good working order at all times.”_

Transport Malta’s policy direction is about safety + quality of service. Removing premium categories for a visibly damaged vehicle is _consistent_ with that – we’re raising, not lowering, the standard applied to passenger-facing service quality.

So from a local law perspective, there’s no prohibition on a booking platform applying stricter aesthetic/quality thresholds than the minimum regulatory level, as long as:

* The car still meets safety/roadworthiness rules (VRT, etc.), and
* Our actions don’t amount to some hidden discrimination.

+*In conclusion:*+
Under the Malta [Service Provider Platform Terms|https://bolt.eu/en-mt/legal/tnc-service-provider/?category=rides], a Driver’s right to access any given Category only exists for so long as they meet the applicable Category requirements. Once a vehicle has visible accident damage, it no longer meets the external-condition requirements for our higher-priced Categories in Malta, so under sections 3.4.4 and 5.20–5.21 we’re entitled to withdraw access to those Categories while the issue persists.

We are not disabling his access to the Bolt Platform – we’re simply limiting him to the basic Category until the car is repaired. That’s a proportionate quality/brand measure and is also fully aligned with our obligation to avoid harm to the integrity and reputation of the platform.

Legal risk is low provided we:
- keep photo evidence of the visible damage;
- have a clear document process for this. Something evidencing that this is not a subjective decision and it is part of a process that in fact exists.
- clearly tell him why the Categories were removed and what he needs to do (repair + photos / re-inspection) to get them back; and
- remind him that, if he disagrees, he can use the internal complaint-handling system described in section 16.8 of the Terms.

This is consistent with S.L. 499.68, which expects LPTVs used for hire to be maintained to a decent standard – we’re raising quality above the regulatory floor, not undermining it.

So yes, in our view the Team can maintain the restriction and refuse to re-enable the high-value categories until the vehicle has been properly repaired, as long as we have photo evidence of the damage (in case we need to prove that this was an objective decision).

Thanks for sharing this. 

Before anything else, we’d need a bit more clarity on a few points:

* Purpose and use of results: could you please confirm what the main objective is? For example:
- Is it primarily to test understanding (do drivers know how Score works, what affects it, how it impacts them)? Or is it to help decide whether to change / keep / remove specific features?
It’s important that the invite text and the survey itself match the real purpose. If expectations are created that _“we’ll change things if you don’t like them”_ but we cannot commit to that, it may damage trust and be used against us later.
* What commitment (if any) are we making to drivers?
- Are we planning to share any high-level results with drivers (e.g. _“this is what we heard, this is what we’re doing about it”_)?
- If the majority of respondents dislike certain features but those are business-critical and we intend to keep them, how do we plan to communicate that?
It would be good to have a basic comms plan so we don’t end up in a situation where we ask for opinions and then visibly ignore them.

From a Malta/legal standpoint, the idea of a survey itself is fine (it doesn’t create new obligations or change the classification of drivers) but we should be transparent and realistic about what we will do with the answers.

My suggestion would be:
- Frame the survey explicitly as a comprehension and feedback exercise (e.g. _“we want to make sure Driver Score is clear and fair, and your feedback will help us improve communication and, where feasible, the feature itself”_);
- Avoid wording that suggests drivers are “voting” on whether the feature stays or goes; and
- Plan at least a short follow-up message to drivers summarising key learnings and any changes we will make (even if small, e.g. better FAQs, clearer in-app explanations).
- Once we have clarity on the points above (purpose and use of results, tool/privacy), I’m happy to re-confirm whether we see any remaining risk in sending it out.

Thank you!

h3. *Summary of Exalate Testing*

Testing was conducted between the Bolt sandbox Jira instance and the new boltexternal instance using both Basic and Visual connection modes. Three projects were created in each environment, with most tests focused on L10N due to its complex custom field and component requirements.

The Basic mode supported only manual syncing with limited fields, while the Visual mode (still in beta) enabled broader field mapping but lacked support for syncing components without custom scripting. Although connections were established successfully, several critical limitations were identified:

* *Licensing constraints:* Cross-instance syncing requires paid licenses on both sides. A paid license on only one instance does not unlock paid features on the other, meaning we would need to purchase a large user-tier license for the main Bolt instance.
* *Feature limitations:* Components cannot be synced using Visual mode unless implemented via script mode, which would require significant setup and maintenance effort.
* *Stability concerns:* Syncing large boards (e.g., 10k+ issues) showed signs of instability and cannot guarantee reliable performance.

Due to these blockers—licensing costs, missing field support, required scripting effort, and instability—Exalate is not suitable for our current needs.

The issue occurs if PNPM decides to fallback to building RocksDB from sources and not to use the pre-build binaries. The issue is caused by the hardening of default C++ compiler options, which doesn’t include {{cstdint}} implicitly anymore. RocksDB already fixed this in recent versions, so an upgrade will fix it for sure.

A workaround exists: force {{cstdint}} inclusion through compiler flags, but it’s merely a hack. I wouldn’t rely on it, better fix it the right way.

Also it’s unclear why it happened in my local env, but not in Jenkins (also running Linux). Maybe I upgraded my c++ faster than our runtime env. So I wouldn’t wait too long, maybe we’ll get a nasty surprise soon with Jenkins.

[~accountid:712020:ed2533e0-41fa-49c6-9812-aa965d995be0]  context on normalization


h1. 📘 *Developer Explanation: Normalizing Average Rating Toward Sample Size*

When you calculate an average rating for multiple restaurants, you _should not_ simply average their ratings.
Instead, you must *weight each restaurant’s rating by how many samples (orders/ratings) it has*.

This prevents a restaurant with very few orders from disproportionately affecting the result.

----

h1. ✅ 1. *Weighted Average Formula (text)*

{noformat}AverageRating = (rating1 * sample1 + rating2 * sample2 + rating3 * sample3)
                / (sample1 + sample2 + sample3)
{noformat}

Where:

* *ratingX* = the restaurant’s average rating
* *sampleX* = the number of orders or individual rating samples
* Ratings with more samples influence the final score more

----

h1. ✅ 2. *How It Works (conceptually)*

The idea:

* A rating based on *many samples* is more reliable.
* A rating based on *few samples* is less reliable.

So the formula multiplies each rating by its sample size to calculate how much it should contribute to the final aggregate score.

----

h1. ⚙️ 3. *Step-by-Step Logic*

h3. Step 1 — Convert each restaurant’s rating into a “total score contribution”

{noformat}scoreX = ratingX * sampleX
{noformat}

This tells you how many “rating points” the restaurant contributes overall.

Example:
If a restaurant has *4.8* rating from *100* orders → score = 480.

----

h3. Step 2 — Sum all score contributions

{noformat}totalScore = score1 + score2 + score3
{noformat}

This gives a combined rating score across all restaurants.

----

h3. Step 3 — Sum all samples

{noformat}totalSamples = sample1 + sample2 + sample3
{noformat}

This gives the total number of orders/ratings across all restaurants.

----

h3. Step 4 — Divide score by samples to get the normalized average

{noformat}AverageRating = totalScore / totalSamples
{noformat}

This ensures restaurants with more data influence the final result more.

----

h1. 🎯 4. *Developer Example Using Your Data*

Restaurants:

||Restaurant||Rating||Orders (samples)||
|1|4.8|100|
|2|4.3|118|
|3|3.3|56|

h3. Step-by-step:

{noformat}score1 = 4.8 * 100 = 480
score2 = 4.3 * 118 = 507.4
score3 = 3.3 * 56  = 184.8
{noformat}

{noformat}totalScore = 480 + 507.4 + 184.8 = 1172.2
totalSamples = 100 + 118 + 56 = 274

AverageRating = 1172.2 / 274 = 4.279
{noformat}

----

h1. 🔍 5. *Why this matters*

* Prevents small-sample restaurants from skewing results
* Produces a stable and comparable rating
* Standard method used in ranking, scoring, and recommendation systems

----

h1. 🧪 6. *Where developers use this*

* Ranking restaurants in listings
* Showing “average rating in an area/segment”
* Machine learning features (aggregate quality features)
* Data quality normalization
* Weighted KPI dashboards

Hi [~accountid:712020:60da7793-200e-4a92-a78d-1705c6e5cdf8] , on top of what [~accountid:712020:02e8ad5d-a35d-44b9-b445-6111cdb230dc] pointed out, I’d like to add something from a privacy POV:

About this:

{quote} Let’s say that all that complete 300 finished rides in XX amount of time automatically enrol into the lottery to win vouchers from our partners (car wash, spare parts) and small technical items, such as headphones, etc.{quote}

*My recommendation would be not to enrol drivers automatically.*

Even if we already collect ride data, using it for competition eligibility is a new context, and drivers should actively agree to participate before that data is used this way. It’s also clearer and fairer from a UX standpoint.

What I’d suggest to stay privacy-aligned:

* Require opt-in before any data is used for ranking or eligibility - this sets clear expectations and avoids surprises later
* Communicate clearly in the opt-in form:
** how performance will be tracked
** what data will be used (e.g. ride count over a fixed period)
** how and when prizes will be awarded
* Avoid automatic enrollment based on activity alone, always let drivers confirm participation
* Use specific, understandable language, e.g.

{quote}"Drivers who opt in and complete 300+ rides between [start date] and [end date] will be entered into a prize draw for vouchers and small tech items."{quote}



If we absolutely want to auto-enrol the drivers:

* We need to inform the drivers that they have been enrolled into the lottery and give information about the rules/how we use their data
*  We need to give option to opt-out, and they will have to be removed from the lottery. We can’t make them participate if they don’t want that

External Legal Counsel provided a recommendation from their side ([12 page doc|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09JY9GFG3T/p1763460565257189]). Read through and highlighted my main concerns to Legal and Privacy:

* External Counsel suggests we rely on legitimate interest and public interest as a legal basis for disclosure of data. However, these are apart of the data protection laws that regulate the processing of personal data (not disclosure to law enforcement). We usually rely on the police law, code of criminal procedure instead.
* External Counsel refers to a court appeal where a judge said the police can investigate through whatever means necessary. This decision is specific to one court case and is not apart of the law.
* Regarding the method of data sharing, the external counsel is again suggesting that the police can investigate through whatever means necessary and we should comply with whatsapp, phone or personal email.

To conclude, they lack knowledge of Privacy and only suggestion is to comply to maintain good relationships.

# “From soundcheck to sunrise. Ride with Bolt.” - This works best for the GhUD Park environment. It carries festival energy and matches the flow of the night; people arriving early and staying late. It’s still more of a general campaign line, but it aligns better with the on-site experience than the others.
# “Accra’s out tonight. You should be, too.”
This works well for comms (absolutely stealing this for push messages), but at the venue it becomes redundant as attendees are already “out tonight.” I worry it might feel slightly mismatched to their real-time context.

My main hesitation is that these lines feel more suited for *citywide OOH promoting the event or general nightlife*, rather than messaging intended for people who are already _inside the venue_.

We really liked these options:

# Brunch → Concert → After-party → Bolt.
# Next stop: anywhere
# Let’s get you to your next party

We’re happy to move forward with options that carry the same vibe. 🙏🏽

Thanks for escalating, and sorry for the inconvenience - the client should not have received these comms, as we have set up guardrails not to send comms if the remaining amount to pay is below 700 KES (5 EUR equivalent). However, there is an issue in the setup logic that caused this to happen. We've already added temporary guardrails and added the client to a list, so they shouldn't receive those debt comms until the situation is fully fixed.

*@user-U024H2C70JK* - Remember, when we added the {{Business Aggregated Invoice Payment Received}} event, we also added {{remaining_amount_to_pay}} and {{currency}} properties to that event, so we could set those thresholds and exclude users if it's below a 5EUR equivalent. Can we add the same 2 event properties to the {{Business Aggregated Invoice Overdue}} event as well - this way we can add those thresholds to our entry criteria as well, and won't even enrol them to our comms, if the remaining amount is below a set limit.

Right now, *Payment Received* is set as an exit condition in the *Invoice Overdue* journey. If a user pays their invoice and the remaining balance is below the threshold, they exit the journey.
However, the limitation is this: if a *partial payment* is made _before_ the *Overdue* event triggers, the user will still enter the journey, but won’t exit, because the payment event happened before enrollment, and exit criteria don’t look back to events that occurred earlier.
We can add a blanket exclusion so that users who have made partial payments within the last 15 days don’t receive communications. However, since payment terms vary, this only applies to the 15-day payment-term group (the most common one, if I remember correctly).
This is why we need those events added to the {{Business Aggregated Invoice Overdue}} event: so users who partially paid _before_ the invoice becomes overdue won’t enter the journey at all. Then, for users who partially pay _after_ the invoice is overdue, the {{Business Aggregated Invoice Payment Received}} event can still be used as the exit condition.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

*RH Low & Moderate Course - Updated*

Hi team! I have re-uploaded all SCORMs for the Low/Moderate Safety modules in TalentLMS and Docebo. I reviewed every file to ensure it matches current processes. Changes are mostly minor: small design adjustments (like text alignment, removing the button mention in the last block of the module), a couple of typo fixes, and one broken link repaired.Some process changes were also updated where I spotted training mismatches after the KB was updated:

* *Trip anomaly* – Updated information about the trip anomaly feature. A CS case is now created only when the user requests to create one. Previously, a case was also created if the user didn’t interact with the pop-up to confirm they were OK.
* *Beehive case statuses* – Updated the section about Beehive case statuses. For _Open_ status, this info was added to the KB: “Open cases that you haven't updated will be moved to Backlog from My Assigned automatically after you change your status to offline. It is possible to submit a case as Open, and it can remain Open until a solution is offered.”
* *Description of one EC* – The _Driver Needed Medical Attention During Journey_ EC description was updated. Previously, it was described as a medical event that required intervention from medical services. Now the mention of medical intervention has been removed: “An event in which the driver suffered a medical event such as a heart attack, seizures, falling unconscious, or any other medical condition.”

*Important!* I kept all response examples the same, where each block was sent as a separate message, since none of the managers [confirmed|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C094LAUST4P/p1764676384217259] that the old format is wrong.I have also marked the last update date in the TD [master|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1UId6GFz8DD7uMcwwd7P_a--zqWYHRtAa-dK8fhIgd1A/edit?gid=338376684#gid=338376684] file.

Identity Center API doesn’t give the user status, therefore I can’t get disabled users.
Via API, I got the list of 290 users not assigned to any groups and deleted them:


{noformat}aws identitystore list-users \
  --identity-store-id d-996771582c \
  --output json > all_users.json

jq -r '.Users[] | "\(.UserId)\t\(.UserName)"' all_users.json > all_users.tsv
###
aws identitystore list-groups \
  --identity-store-id d-996771582c \
  --output json > all_groups.json

jq -r '.Groups[].GroupId' all_groups.json > group_ids.txt

###
: > group_members_user_ids_raw.txt

while IFS= read -r G; do
  echo "Fetching members for group $G"

  aws identitystore list-group-memberships \
    --identity-store-id d-996771582c \
    --group-id "$G" \
    --output json > "group_${G}.json"

  jq -r '.GroupMemberships[].MemberId.UserId' "group_${G}.json" >> group_members_user_ids_raw.txt
done < group_ids.txt
###
sort -u group_members_user_ids_raw.txt > group_members_user_ids.txt
###
awk -v OFS='\t' '
  NR==FNR { seen[$1]=1; next }
  {
    uid = $1
    user = $2
    if (!(uid in seen)) {
      print uid, user
    }
  }
' group_members_user_ids.txt all_users.tsv > users_without_groups.tsv
###
while IFS=$'\t' read -r IIC_USER_ID IIC_USERNAME; do
  echo "Deleting $IIC_USERNAME ($IIC_USER_ID)"
  aws identitystore delete-user \
    --identity-store-id d-996771582c \
    --user-id "$IIC_USER_ID"
done < users_without_groups-2025-12-04.tsv{noformat}

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Hi [~accountid:63abfbf46f068efec8f6b8f8], thank you for providing the order form with the terms of the contract.

+Questions regarding the context+: 

* What do you mean by unintentionally?
* When did the agency contact you and what was the content of their message?



+Legal position+:

* The trailer was used outside the scope of rights granted (support → festival/public event ≠ digital), outside the contractual term (post-1-year duration), and without renewal. KOM’s clause (Article 8) does not grant full rights ownership, and explicitly states that only limited diffusion rights are granted upon payment. This is therefore an unauthorised use which exposes Bolt to a claim for infringement. 
* However, you say that the use was unintentional, brief (3 days), and had low exposure (1M vs. 35M). Article 11 gives them the right to claim damages if there’s a breach, but these must be proportionate to the prejudice (i.e. actual harm, usage, market rate).



+Negotiation of Damages+:

* Original actor rights: €300/actor/year → €600 total + Contractual Year 2 renewal is +5% = €315/actor. Based on this logic, continued usage should follow similar pricing logic, which would make the market reference at €315/actor/year.
* The damages for a 3 day overuse could be calcuted on a daily basis so (€315 ÷ 365) × 3 = ~€2.59/day/actor → ~€15.50 total (€31 for tawo actors). Even if you add a “penalty” multiplier (e.g. x10 for lack of clearance), you’re at ~€310 max. 
* They’re asking €1,600 total (i.e. €800/actor), which is 2.5x higher than Year 1 rights, for a use 90% smaller in visibility and 0.8% of the time. This lacks proportionality.
* I think that offering 500€ would be a fair settlement. 


Let’s discuss this further on our call today. 

Thanks

h1. Battery cycle count by HW version

An overview of battery cycle counts by hardware version shows that most batteries have completed fewer than 100 cycles.

!image-20251204-130824.png|width=786,alt="image-20251204-130824.png"!

h1. New handle strap feedback

Oslo is currently the only city that have received Dragon batteries (HW version U1) featuring the looped handle-strap design. Feedback from this market indicates that only 1% of the female connector membranes are damaged.

This rate is significantly lower than the average damage rate of 33%, taking into consideration that the U1 batteries have undergone fewer cycles than other hardware versions.

A comparison between Germany (old handle strap design) and Oslo (new handle strap design) shows that batteries equipped with the new handle strap exhibit better connector condition. In Oslo, there is no visible connector wear, whereas many German connectors show consistent wear patterns along the front edge of the connector.

Example: Oslo D2 female connector

!image-20251204-140357.png|width=282,alt="image-20251204-140357.png"!

Example: female connector in Germany

!image-20251204-140605.png|width=213,alt="image-20251204-140605.png"!

h1. Connector testing

A controlled test was conducted with three batteries:

*Battery 1:* Inserted as intended (rear end first) and removed with the front end cap first.
Result: _No signs of wear after 100 cycles._

!image-20251204-142341.png|width=288,alt="image-20251204-142341.png"!

*Battery 2:* Inserted incorrectly (female connector first) and removed rear-end first.
Result: Wear appeared after 30 cycles, similar to what is observed in Germany. After 60 cycles the wear became significant, though the membrane did not break.

!image-20251204-141440.png|width=381,alt="image-20251204-141440.png"!

*Battery 3:* Inserted incorrectly (same as Battery 2).
Result: Significant wear appeared after 30 cycles, and the membrane broke at that point.

!image-20251204-141615.png|width=371,alt="image-20251204-141615.png"!

h1. Conclusion

The findings clearly show that incorrect handling during installation and removal leads to female connector wear and eventual membrane failure.

The new looped handle-strap design substantially reduces the likelihood of mishandling, leading to better connector condition and lower failure rates.

Next steps include creating an SOP for local replacement of female connectors, aligning with LOPS to assign a dedicated battery repair person in each warehouse, and ensuring that all batteries are reworked to the new looped handle-strap design.

* There are no service levels or details about tech support in the website Terms. 

__________________________________________________________________________

*Most important points from the Terms* 

* *Modification at any time.*  Pipedrive can modify the Terms at any time. Changes will be effective at the earlier of (i) the first Renewal Date following posting, or (ii) thirty (30) days after posting. 

_Explanation_: It’s risky in a sense that Bolt will not be able to negotiate these changes. 

* *Client can terminate the agreement at any time* 

_Explanation:_ just FYI, in favour of Bolt 

*  *Limitation of Liability* 

_Explanation:_ Pipedrive’s liability is limited to *6 months fees* which is very low liability limit considering the fees that we will be paying. It is not enough to cover Bolt from potential damages. cc [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] 

* *Exclusion of Consequential and Related Damages.* Pipedrive is not liable for any indirect damages (e.g. legal fees, court proceedings fees), loss of data. cc [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] 
* *No liability for loss, corruption of data.* Pipedrive will not be liable to the Client for deletion of, corruption of, or failure to store any Client Data. cc [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] 

_Explanation:_ due to business sensitivity of AV projects data this is a high risk for Bolt. 

* *No warranties*. Pipedrive disclaims all warranties about accuracy, non-infringement of the tool. 

_Explanation:_ quite standard disclaimer for SaaS but still highlighting FYI 

* *Usage of Client Data.* During or after the use of the Pipedrive Services by Client, Pipedrive may, and Client hereby instructs Pipedrive to, anonymize or aggregate Client Data and use such anonymized or aggregated data for any purpose.

Explanation:  risky clause for Bolt because it’s not stated that Pipedrive is obliged to anonymize or aggregate the data, only if Bolt instructs to do so. cc [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] 

* *For InfoSec information.* It’s forbidden to perform any security or penetration testing of the Pipedrive Services or Pipedrive Materials 
* *AI.*  Pipedrive may share Inputs and Outputs (including Client Data) with AI Service Providers, such as OpenAI, LLC (“*OpenAI*”), to facilitate the provision of AI Functionality.

Explanation: high risk clause for Bolt. It means that Bolt’s data can be leaked into AI provider’s database. There is not opt out opportunity for this, so we shouldn’t use AI services of Pipedrive to ensure we don’t expose Bolt’s data to such risk. cc [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] 

* *Automatic Renewal.* Each Subscription will automatically renew for *successive renewal Subscription Terms (1 month or 1 year),* unless terminated with a specific notice 

_Explanation: Bolt’s preferable solution is to have_ a defined subscription period without automatic renewal.
Conclusion: no breach on Bolt’s side. I will add a summary and conclusion of the case when workload permits it.

It took 12 mins on {{rd-fleet.xlarge}} 1-8 workers:

{noformat}
with t1 as (
  select
    fu.created_date,
    date_trunc('hour', fu.created) as created_hour,
    fu.city_id,
    fu.session_id,
    cast(
      get_json_object(fu.feature_config, '$.driver_utilisation') as double
    ) as driver_utilisation,
    cast(get_json_object(fu.feature_config, '$.user_control_pred') as double) as pred_s2o_baseline,
    cast(get_json_object(fu.feature_config, '$.user_treatment_pred') as double) as pred_s2o,
    cast(get_json_object(fu.feature_config, '$.s2hco_elasticity') as double) as s2hco_elasticity,
    cast(get_json_object(fu.feature_config, '$.user_change_pct') as double) as price_change,
    from_json(
      get_json_object(feature_config, '$.processed_features'),
      'array<struct<
        net_rate:double,
        net_rate_before_dc:double
      >>'
    ) as pf_array
  from
    sel_rides_spark.feature_usage fu
  where
    fu.feature_name = 'multiarmed-dynamic-commissions'
    and fu.created_date between date '2025-11-26 12:00:00' and date '2025-12-03 23:00:00'
    and fu.city_id in (344,456,813)
    and fu.auth_type = "price_prediction_token"
    and cast(get_json_object(fu.feature_config, '$.model_applied') as boolean)
    and not cast(get_json_object(fu.feature_config, '$.applied_exploration') as boolean)
),
t2 as (
  select
    * except (pf_array, pf),
    pf.net_rate,
    pf.net_rate_before_dc,
    100 * (pf.net_rate - pf.net_rate_before_dc) as net_rate_gap_pp
  from
    t1
    lateral view explode(t1.pf_array) exploded as pf
)
select
  sc.name as city_name,
  t2.city_id,
  min(t2.created_date) as first_date,
  max(t2.created_date) as last_date,
  avg(
    case
      when t2.price_change > 0 then 1
      else 0
    end
  ) as extract_rate,
  avg(
    case
      when t2.price_change < 0 then 1
      else 0
    end
  ) as invest_rate,
  avg(t2.price_change) / 100 as avg_price_change,
  avg(
    case
      when t2.price_change > 0 then t2.price_change
      else null
    end
  ) / 100 as avg_price_change_when_extract,
  avg(
    case
      when t2.price_change < 0 then t2.price_change
      else null
    end
  ) / 100 as avg_price_change_when_invest,
  avg(
    case
      when t2.net_rate_gap_pp > 1 then 1
      else 0
    end
  ) as rolling_net_rate_gap_above_1pp,
  avg(
    case
      when t2.net_rate_gap_pp < -1 then 1
      else 0
    end
  ) as rolling_net_rate_gap_below_1pp,
  avg(t2.net_rate_gap_pp) as avg_rolling_net_rate_gap_pp
from
  t2
    inner join ng_public_spark.admin_system_city sc
      on sc.id = t2.city_id
group by
  1,
  2{noformat}

with that query
{code}WITH all_violations AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT
        b1.id AS block_id,
        b1.entity_type,
        b1.entity_id,
        b1.reason_id
    FROM block_block b1
    JOIN block_block b2
        ON b1.entity_id = b2.entity_id
       AND b1.reason_id = b2.reason_id
       AND b1.id < b2.id
       AND b1.start < b2.end
       AND b2.start < b1.end
       AND b1.start < b1.end
       AND b2.start < b2.end
       AND b1.end IS NOT NULL
       AND b2.end IS NOT NULL
    JOIN block_reason r
        ON r.id = b1.reason_id
       AND (
           r.isolation = 'reason'
           OR
           (
               r.isolation = 'sub_reason'
               AND r.sub_reason_name IS NOT NULL
               AND get_json_object(b1.data, concat('$.', r.sub_reason_name))  = get_json_object(b2.data, concat('$.', r.sub_reason_name))
           )
       )
),

total_blocks AS (
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_count FROM block_block
),

total_violations AS (
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_violation_count FROM all_violations
),
by_entity_type AS (
    SELECT
        v.entity_type,
        COUNT(*) AS violation_count,
        t.total_count AS total_blocks,
        tv.total_violation_count AS total_violations,
        ROUND(COUNT(*) * 100.0 / t.total_count, 2) AS percent_of_all_blocks,
        ROUND(COUNT(*) * 1.0 / t.total_count, 5) AS ratio_of_all_blocks
    FROM all_violations v
    CROSS JOIN total_blocks t
    CROSS JOIN total_violations tv
    GROUP BY v.entity_type, t.total_count, tv.total_violation_count
)

SELECT * FROM by_entity_type
UNION ALL
SELECT
    'TOTAL' AS entity_type,
    tv.total_violation_count AS violation_count,
    t.total_count AS total_blocks,
    tv.total_violation_count AS total_violations,
    ROUND(tv.total_violation_count * 100.0 / t.total_count, 2) AS percent_of_all_blocks,
    ROUND(tv.total_violation_count * 1.0 / t.total_count, 5) AS ratio_of_all_blocks
FROM total_blocks t
CROSS JOIN total_violations tv
ORDER BY CASE WHEN entity_type = 'TOTAL' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, entity_type;{code}

However, from what I understand this is basically category access based on KPIs.

In fact, our view is that this feature may undermine key elements of Bolt’s reclassification defense strategy because:

* Bolt determines *access to additional earning opportunities* based on *performance metrics*
* Bolt generally *controls drivers’ access to rides*

Despite not affecting basic platform access, the feature creates platform-controlled, performance-based differentiation, which is a hallmark of subordinate employment relationships.

This was assessed centrally, and central legal indicated key elements of feature de-risking:

* Selection of *applicable KPIs* has *main impact on the risk level* of the access restriction
** _The lowest risk KPI - completed/ finished rides_
** _The medium risk KPI - DS_
** _High but not the worst - acceptance rates_
** _The highest - online hours_
* Do not use *invisible metrics* (e.g. driver ratings not visible to drivers) as *eligibility criteria* for category access
* The *standard category* must always *remain unaffected*
* As a general principle, if KPIs are used to regulate access to categories, the following questions help strengthen legal defensibility:
** Is the KPI *necessary and decisive* for the *category to function* because the *rider pays more for the category*, and is that *higher price linked to specific service criteria*?

_Example: a low cancellation rate may be required for scheduled rides, because riders pay more and expect reliability (no last-minute cancellations)._

{quote}Dear [name],

Thank you for your follow-up. We have reviewed your request again in light of the points you raised.

We appreciate that you are not asking for the identity of any passenger. However, the right of access under the UK GDPR is not an unconditional entitlement to all information that contains your personal data. Article 15(4) UK GDPR expressly allows a controller to refuse access where providing the data would adversely affect the rights and freedoms of others.

In the context of ratings and free-text comments, disclosure carries a real risk of re-identification. Even when names or contact details are removed, the combination of trip ID, date and time, the rating given, and the wording or context of a comment is often enough for a driver to determine which passenger left the feedback. Drivers are physically present during each trip and typically remember who they transported at a particular moment, especially where the trip was unusual, took place during quieter periods, or involved a memorable interaction. Sharing this information would therefore undermine the ability of passengers to provide candid feedback without fear of retaliation. As set out in Bolt’s Privacy Notices, protecting this feedback mechanism is a necessary safeguard for users’ rights.

For these reasons, and in line with Article 15(4) UK GDPR, Bolt cannot provide the trip-level breakdown of ratings, timestamps or free-text comments.

In addition, the right of access does not require Bolt to generate new datasets or restructure existing internal data, including creating a historical breakdown of individual rating events where such a dataset does not already exist in that format.

You already have access to the personal data that can be safely provided: your overall average rating, which reflects all recent trips in accordance with our standard calculation method. Should you wish to have access to any other data, such as your entire order history, we would be happy to facilitate that.

Please note that this is our final position on the scope of your access request. If you have any further privacy-related questions, please let us know.

Sincerely,

Bolt{quote}

Dear [~accountid:712020:7a4efde6-3133-4524-b558-93557ebd60e8] 

Thank you again for the productive call last week.

As discussed, the main issue with the agreement is that it treats Bolt as a *data processor*, not a *data controller*. This matters because a processor has to follow every instruction from the customer about how their data is handled. Some of those requirements would be very difficult — or even impossible — for Bolt to carry out in practice.

There is also an important legal point: if Bolt is viewed as a processor and cannot follow a customer request, *the law does not allow us to limit our liability*, even if the contract says otherwise. This creates a higher risk for Bolt.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
We have an explanation of why this is problematic and how the roles differ here:

{panel}

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.

I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

* *TRT*
**  We observed a *drop in overall TRT*, which appears to correlate strongly with improvements in CSAT and a reduction in reopen rate.
* *ATHT*
**  ATHT decreased, which contrasts with initial expectations that it would rise. However, the reduction in reopen rate likely reduced the time spent on returning cases, mitigating the anticipated ATHT increase.
* *Survey Response Rate:*
**  Response rate has also gone up, further improving the reliability of the insight.

Overall, *the actions we have in place appear to be yielding positive results*, as reflected by improvements across several key metrics. At this stage no course correct for actions is required.*Next Steps*

*📅 Update – 4 December 2025*
by: Łukasz Czub - CS Operations Manager - LT, LV, DK

sharing update regarding CSAT pilot for Latvia delivery.
*Note*: Data has been reuploaded today, considering potentially delayed surveys, nevertheless there is still potential impact in the coming days from cases that are resolved at later stage.
*Key Observations*

* *CSAT Impact*
** The Pilot group CSAT remains significantly elevated, now showing *continued and increasing deviation from the non-pilot group*, which indicates that the actions implemented within the pilot are delivering sustained impact.
**  Overall CSAT performance remains positive, with both pilot and non-pilot groups improving, though the _pilot group continues to outpace the average score meaningfully while non-pilot group improvement have slow down._
* *Reopen Rate*
** We have observed a *further decrease in reopen rate specifically within the pilot group*, reinforcing the strong correlation between lower reopen rates and higher CSAT scores. This trend supports the hypothesis that improved first-time resolution quality is driving customer satisfaction gains.
* *TRT*
** After the data reupload, we observed a noticeable spike in TRT for Week 47. Nevertheless, what gives us confidence is that the *pilot group reversed this trend compared to the overall average and successfully decreased TRT for handled cases*. This further reinforces the positive impact of the ongoing pilot actions.
* *ATHT*
** ATHT have observed an increase in Week 47 most likely due to higher focus on customer resolution, nevertheless have decreased in Week 48. We will continue to observe ATHT as a metric, nevertheless so far we have not observed Pilot driven significant variations.
* *Survey Response Rate*
** Survey response rates remain elevated and increase week over week, providing higher-confidence insight into customer experience trends and further validating the observed improvements.

*Summary*
The actions currently in place continue to yield positive and sustained results, as shown by performance divergence between the pilot and non-pilot groups, improved CSAT, and reduced reopen rates. At this stage, *no course correction is required.*
*Next Steps*

* We will continue all implemented actions throughout this and the following week. Based on sustained impact and stability of results, we will determine whether the pilot should proceed to *Phase 2*, introducing the *Agent Empowerment* action.
* Two outlier agents within Pilot group are undergoing performance improvement plans, as we aimed to keep the group diverse in terms of performance buckets, we want to observe impact of continous improvement cycles implemented within pilot group.

* Bolt couriers pick up from pharmacy but act as _agent of Liki24/pharmacy for delivery_.

* The _pharmacy_ is the seller
* But the _provider on Bolt Food is Liki24_
* Liki24 *is not the seller*

Hello Eva,

{quote}Merci pour ton mail ! J'ai tenté de te joindre sur ton tél pro.

J'aurais aimé pouvoir te dire ce qui va suivre par téléphone mais le temps passe et nous devons régulariser la situation au plus vite.

Je comprends votre point de vue, mais même s'il s'agit d'une situation non intentionnelle, les faits sont là : vous avez diffusé une vidéo dont les droits avaient été négociés pour le web uniquement. Et encore une fois, c'est justement votre bonne foi qui fait que les comédiens acceptent des sommes très raisonnables au vu du contexte.

Il faut aussi savoir que le tarif initial des droits - 300€ HT - était vraiment très bas, mais nous souhaitions, KÖM et les comédiens, faire ce pas afin que la collab se réalise, et on a bien fait !! 

Cependant, cette somme n'aurait jamais été envisageable si nous avions su en amont qu'il y allait avoir 35M d'impressions.

De plus cette année, le syndicat des mannequins/comédiens a augmenté son minimum légal et ils n'accepteront pas le tarif de 500€ HT chacun en étant hors d'un scope déjà très bas. 

Concernant Frédérika, j'ai pu négocier ses droits à 600€ HT, je ne pourrai pas aller plus bas. 

Je sais que la situation peut paraitre injuste, mais elle l'est tout autant pour les comédiens qui ont vu leur image exploitée sans leur consentement. 

1M d'impressions en 3 jours d'événement public, ça peut se rémunérer bien plus que ce que nous avons pu négocier, mais j'ai fais mon maximum pour que les comédiens acceptent un prix raisonnable, justement dans cette logique de bonne foi. Je peux t'assurer que nous sommes sur des comédiens qui la jouent fair-play. 

Cela fait maintenant une semaine qu'ils attendent leur contrat, et je me fais relancer. Il faut que la situation se régularise dans la journée. 

Le risque de faire trop durer est que les comédiens peuvent tout à fait se retourner et demander plus, et ils sont dans leur droit tant que rien n'a été signé.

Enfin, je rappelle que KÖM ne touche pas un centime dans cette histoire, le montant des droits est intégralement reversé au comédien (c'est la loi). En revanche, si la négociation n'aboutit pas aujourd'hui, je serai dans l'obligation de facturer le temps passé sur ce sujet, c'est que nous faisons habituellement…

J'espère que tu comprends qu'il n'y a aucune volonté de notre part de vous estorquer une somme de manière injustifiée, mais bien au contraire de vous accompagner au mieux et que ce soit juste. Il faut être très vigilant lors de la diffusion de vidéos lorsqu'il y a des acteurs, et que vous le fassiez consciemment ou pas ne change en réalité rien à la situation finale.

[~accountid:712020:b3dbddb5-16a8-4ad6-9138-80fbe6e695a9], given that biometric data used for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person qualifies as a _special category of personal data_ under Article 9 GDPR, we unfortunately *cannot rely on legitimate interest under Article 6* to justify this processing. Legitimate interest is not an available derogation under Article 9, and therefore cannot lift the prohibition on processing biometric identifiers for verification.

To proceed lawfully, we would need to rely on one of the explicit Article 9(2) exemptions. In our case, the only viable option is *explicit consent* from the user. This must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous, and we must also ensure that refusal does not lead to detriment - otherwise the consent wouldn’t be considered freely given.

Practically, this means implementing:

* *explicit, opt-in consent* before we process any biometric data; and
* *a fallback manual verification route* for users who choose not to consent.

This approach aligns with GDPR requirements while still enabling us to meet the urgent regulatory demands around identity verification. We also follow the same approach for selfie age verifications in rentals.

Happy to discuss further or help outline the consent and fallback flows.

We are going to update the records directly.

We are doing this, as an exception, for two reasons:

# {color:#ff5630}*Reissuing the records will not solve the problem,*{color} as the problem happens when the aggregated provider/courier invoice is generated. Issuing another record with the correct external ID will not stop the record from existing there.
# {color:#ff5630}*Invoice External ID is an implementation detail:*{color} the records themselves are correct and do not need to be reissued. The only problem is that they are being picked up to be used on the wrong invoice. The invoices have also not been generated with the coupon record.

h2. Alternatives Considered 

* {color:#36b37e}*Temporary code changes:*{color} We could do a temporary code change to ignore the coupon records and then rerun the tasks. I am against that because it leaves the database in an inconsistent state. Also, it becomes less traceable: after someone analyses the data, it will be impossible to judge why these records were not processed, since the code changes would be gone. [~accountid:623ace301c7f6a00704940a2], thanks for raising these points. We are currently working on revising our CCTV policy, so your suggestions are very helpful. To address your question on ownership: CCTV policy and retention standards fall under the Privacy team. 

Regarding the issues you highlighted:

*1. Footage retention*

The revised internal policy will set the default retention period to *7 days*. This is a very common benchmark for general security. However, some national requirements (like in Austria/Germany - 72h) lean towards shorter times, emphasising immediate need.

If you believe 7 days is still insufficient for a particular market, please outline the operational reasons and scenarios requiring longer storage. Any extension beyond 7 days would need separate approval from the Privacy team.

*2. Risk of losing footage*

If extended retention isn’t feasible, we can work with Risk & Compliance team and the relevant operational owners to define a clear process for immediate download and preservation of footage following an incident.

*3. Single-person access dependency*

The updated policy will allow for the possibility of granting access to an additional authorised person, but this must be assessed building by building.

*Current criteria for higher deposits and booking prevention on premium cars:* User age, time of the day, day of the week



*Experiment:* dynamic deposit lifted for all Users whose driving score is above 30, i.e. reward good driving habits.

*Privacy risk:* low

# Rewarding good behavior → Driving score improves user experience
# No high-risk profiling → Doesn’t affect users' ability to access services
# No ADM with legal or significant effects → System removes barriers
# Users won’t be informed of the experiment → wighted out by short duration
