h2. 🌳 *CSRD Update* — social metrics workshops & regulatory news

h3. 🦡 *CSRD progress*

*Social metrics walkthrough:* The first KPMG social metrics workshop has taken place; the second is scheduled for *Dec 10 (2–4 PM)*. Invitations and attendance tiers (required vs. optional) have been fully updated.

*Key takeaways from Workshop #1:*

* *Sustainability:* Double Materiality Assessment will be updated next year to formally include *S2 (value chain workers)*, particularly couriers and drivers. Documenting & developing ESG controls is a major 2026 project.
* *People:* Improving Diversity & Inclusion data detail, clarifying contingent worker identification (currently via Okta), and moving updated Collective Bargaining data into Workday for auditability.
* *General:* All numeric metric owners must justify *margins of error* in methodology descriptions per ESRS.
* *Agreement:* Workforce calculations will use *FY end (31 Dec)* numbers.
* *Systems:* Discussed Workiva’s Sustainability Reporting program and Workday → Data Warehouse → Workiva pipeline.

*Peer benchmarking (KPMG):*

* Carrefour considered best-in-class.
* We’ll map country-specific legislation (e.g., German Supply Chain Act, French Duty of Vigilance) similar to other reporters.



h3. 🧩 *Workiva* 

* Workiva hypercare prep for Q1 2026 began in the *first week of December* (Finance Reporting × Sustainability Compliance). First metric data flow tested. People team included for the next session.
* Workiva & Sustainability team had an ESG product feedback session on {{2025-11-19}}



h3. 🏛️ *EU Taxonomy*

* Finance has the necessary data. Budget exists for potential KPMG support workshops in *2025–2026*.
* Climate Risk Assessment offers asked from BIG4 and Sustinere, meetings scheduled for the next week. Currently waiting Finance’s feedback on whether we can ask for an offer from PC too. 



h3. 📰 *EU regulatory news*

The EU Parliament has backed several *CSRD simplifications* (pending final confirmation), including:

* Voluntary sector-specific reporting
* Reduced qualitative disclosure requirements
* No mandatory transition plan
* Protection of small suppliers from excessive information requests
* A new digital reporting portal with templates & guidance

Next step: *Trilogue negotiations* began *Nov 18*; the goal is to finalise by *end of 2025*. 



h3. ❓ *Q&A – What’s the status of the EU Omnibus changes?*

We’re waiting for the EU to confirm which datapoints will be mandatory. Trilogue negotiations are ongoing, with the aim to reach an agreement by year-end (though delays are still possible). Once adopted, the Directive will be published in the Official Journal and enter into force. I’ll update you as soon as the scope and timelines are official.



h3. ⏭️ *What’s next*

* *Dec 10, 2–4 PM* — Social metrics workshop #2
* *Dec 11, 10–12* — Estonian ESG Mastermind (Liisa attending)
* *Dec 16, 4 PM EET* — “Unpacking the Omnibus changes to CSRD & CS3D” webinar (Liisa attending)

Hi [Name],

*Instructions to the outside counsels:*

We require *controller-to-controller (“C2C”) data protection clauses* to ensure compliance with applicable data protection laws, including, inter alia, the Thai data protection laws and the GDPR. Please prepare draft C2C provisions that:
h3. *_A. Clearly establish the controller roles_*
* _Confirm that_ *_each party acts as an independent and separate data controller_* _for the personal data it processes in connection with the services._
* _Clarify that_ *_each party is responsible for its own data protection compliance_*_, including identifying a lawful basis, transparency obligations, data subject rights handling for its own processing, and security measures._
h3. *_B. Limit the scope to necessary processing_*
* _Confirm that personal data may only be shared or processed to the extent necessary for the services._
* _No processing for unrelated or incompatible purposes._
h3. *_C. Liability_*
* _Insert an_ *_aggregate liability cap of EUR 5,000,000 per party_* _for all claims arising from or relating to the data protection clauses._
h3. *_D. Indemnification_*
* _Maintain_ *_mutual indemnification_*_:_
** _Each party indemnifies the other for losses arising from breaches of its own data protection obligations._
h3. *_E. Use the clause below as reference_*
_We attach the clause text to indicate the_ *_tone, structure, and level of detail_* _we expect. Please draft the new C2C clauses to be aligned with this style and level of complexity, but tailored to the specifics of the new partnership:_

{quote}*(a)*
Each Party shall process personal data of the Buyer as an independent and separate data controller. The Merchant and the Bank shall be responsible for compliance with their own data protection obligations with respect to personal data of the Buyer. This applies in particular with regard to the existence of legitimate legal grounds for the processing (in particular transmission and use) of personal data of the Buyer for the purpose of Services contracted by the Merchant.

*(b)*

The Bank will only process personal data and/or transfer such data to third parties where required to provide the Services on a strict need-to-know basis. For the avoidance of doubt, the Merchant is not responsible for the Bank’s data processing as a separate data controller. The Bank shall solely be responsible for its processing activities. If requested by the Merchant, the Bank will provide reasonable assistance with regards to data subject rights requests in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation. Each Party shall put in place adequate security measures to protect any personal data that it processes and shall not do, or omit to do, anything that would breach the General Data Protection Regulation or applicable laws.Following the discovery of a personal data breach affecting personal data obtained in the context of this Agreement, the Bank shall notify the Merchant without undue delay and provide a description and gravity of the personal data breach, along with the steps taken to rectify it.

*(c)*

Each Party (the “Indemnifying Party”) shall, at all times during and after the term of this Agreement, defend, hold harmless, and indemnify the other Party (the “Indemnified Party”) at the Indemnifying Party’s expense, on demand, against any claims, losses, damages, costs, expenses, or other liabilities (including but not limited to legal fees) incurred by the Indemnified Party arising out of or in connection with the Indemnifying Party’s processing of personal data. The Merchant and the Bank shall cooperate in good faith in the defense or settlement of any such claims.{quote}
*Important:* If in your opinion the clauses require additional detail to ensure compliance with applicable law, please do not hesitate to add all of the necessary changes.

*Details re/ privacy risk:*

* *Credit card data* is received by Xendit only in *encrypted form*, which does not identify a data subject. Xendit has *no technical ability to decrypt* the data and cannot deduce the identity of the cardholder. Xendit also *does not have the authority* to request decryption from Bolt.
* *Cardholder full name* is *not transmitted* to Xendit due to Bolt’s technical design and data-minimisation controls.
* As a result, *Xendit does not factually receive any personal data* attributable to a data subject.

*Privacy Approach:*
Given the above, the privacy's current position is to include standard *light-touch controller-to-controller (C2C) clauses*, with:

* *Mutual indemnification*, and
* *Aggregate liability cap of EUR 5 million per party*,
consistent with Bolt’s standard for low-risk data interactions.

*Status:* the Privacy team has supplied *instructions to external legal counsel*, who will proceed with drafting and reviewing the agreement, including the privacy component.

Example for some [Driver|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet/drivers/edit/3318350?tab=profile&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn]:

Taking November 2025 example from [Balance history|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/balanceHistory?balanceHistoryFilterSearch=%7B%22external_id%22%3A3318350%2C%22type%22%3A%22Driver%22%2C%22month%22%3A%7B%22month%22%3A11%2C%22year%22%3A2025%7D%2C%22viewType%22%3A%22monthly%22%2C%22week%22%3A%7B%22start%22%3A1762725600000%2C%22end%22%3A1763330399999%7D%7D]. 

Commission that driver had to pay is

{quote}*Commission = expense_cash_commission* + *expense_commission* (48.50 EUR + 190.83 EUR) = €239.33 EUR{quote}

this commission is ±20% of the amount driver had in Ride fees

{quote}Fees = *earning_in_app_ride_fee* + *earning_cash_ride_fee* (947.70 EUR + 242.50 EUR) = €1,190.20 EUR

Commission % = commission / fees = €239.33 EUR / 1,190.20 EUR = 0.20 = 20%{quote}

the [invoice|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-document/invoices/5649895597?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] was issued for 132.94 euro, which is less than 239.33 because we do *commission netting* in Estonia.

{quote}*What is Commission Netting?*

*Commission netting* is a process used to simplify how drivers are invoiced for commissions, especially when there are bonuses, campaigns, or compensations involved.

*Without Netting:*

Normally, a driver would receive separate invoices:

One for the commission they owe (e.g., 20% of ride fees)

Separate invoices for any bonuses, campaigns, or compensations they receive

*With Netting (as done in Estonia):*

Instead of issuing multiple invoices, the system *reduces the commission amount* by the total value of any bonuses, campaigns, or compensations the driver earned.

The driver receives a *single, lower commission invoice* that already accounts for these discounts.{quote}

You can see discounts earned via cash and app rides in *earning_cash_discount_netted* and *earning_in_app_discount_netted.*

So we can calculate the final netted commission like this:

{quote}Netted Commission = Commission - *earning_cash_discount_netted - earning_in_app_discount_netted* = €239.33 - 26.70 EUR - 79.70 EUR = €132.93{quote}

132.93 is the same amount you can see on Monthly invoice (take invoice from November from [+here+|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients/128179276?tab=partner_invoices&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn])

✨ That’s how you can calculate Commission Netting in Balance history.

{noformat}WITH RankedSyncs AS (
    SELECT
        DATE(created) AS sync_date,
        TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, created, last_update) AS diff,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY DATE(created) ORDER BY TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, created, last_update)) AS row_num,
        COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY DATE(created)) AS total_count
    FROM menu_version_pim_sync_event
    WHERE status = 'completed'
)
SELECT
    sync_date,
    AVG(diff) AS median_diff_secs,
    total_count AS records_processed
FROM RankedSyncs
WHERE row_num IN (FLOOR((total_count + 1) / 2), CEIL((total_count + 1) / 2))
GROUP BY sync_date
ORDER BY sync_date DESC;{noformat}

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


 would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en

Advise the customer to check with their bank to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to 30 days to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

For reference, ARN - the *Allmänna reklamationsnämnden (ARN)* is not a court, but an independent dispute resolution body for consumer issues. Their process is deliberately informal and designed to be accessible, which means they don’t apply the same requirements that an “official investigation” by an authority or a court would. Also, the recommendations made by ARN are *not legally binding*. 

When a company is reported to ARN:

* The company gets the chance to respond to the consumer’s claims. The response doesn’t need to be legally framed - what matters is that the company addresses *all points raised by the consumer*.
** This is explicitly stated on their [website|https://www.arn.se/foretag/].
* ARN bases its assessment only on the written submissions and evidence provided; it doesn’t conduct its own investigation or hearings.

Because ARN is *not a court*, there is no legal requirement for a signed, “official” document - and the response is often submitted directly via the website (that sometimes, CS has access to even).

Hi team, 

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

The uplifts for the selected specification ({{'prior_level_sd' = 0.01}}, {{'train_dur' = 84}}) are in the [doc|https://docs.google.com/document/d/19XxHrcJ0CReDBWJ9QkinGuniaicvOlY35uTtunFRwIQ/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.r6swv3vi15z]. Sessions and orders created results are similar in direction no matter whether we use napkin style analysis or causalimpact. For orders finished though, napkin style shows an uplift unlike causalimpact. It is related to the fact that we only look at a 28 day campaign period in causalimpact as our default setting, while in the napkin analysis we look at a 41 day campaign. The uplift in finished orders is mostly visible after week 4, so the latter approach captures this time period. Please find attached the caualimpact graphs below.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Hi team, any update on this issue?

The reason we see this discrepancy is because for guardrails we did not compute CUPED, but for Hypothesis we did.

Why CUPED matters here? Well, it's because capping depends on test and pre-test data (if pre-test data is available, i.e. CUPED is enabled). But that's for v4 metrics.

For the current metric of interest, which is a v3 metric, the logic is a bit different. If CUPED is enabled, we compute the capping thresholds based on pre-test data. If it is disabled, we compute it based on test data. Here is [where|https://github.com/bolteu/data-experimentation/blob/master/experimentation/experimentation/ab_processor/v3/flows/targeting/processing_plan.py#L126] we do it.

In case of Hypothesis and Carsharing dashboards, CUPED is enabled, so the capping thresholds are calculated based on pre-test data. For guardrails, it's not the case as CUPED is disabled, so the thresholds are calculated only based on test period.

*Bolt Chauffeur Miami Pilot - Project Update (November 2025)*

*Ask to New Members:* To get up to speed, please take a few minutes to scroll through the *previous updates* shared here. These outline the project’s purpose, background, and discovery-phase outcomes.

*1. Recap on Objective*
The Miami pilot is part of the Chauffeur team's broader effort to *define how we launch non-ride-hailing markets* and test what it takes to *enter and operate in the U.S.*, using Miami as a test market.

* *Note*: The goal isn’t necessarily to _launch_ in Q4 but to complete the research, validation, and groundwork needed to build the SOP for future U.S. launches.

# *What’s Been Done So Far*

* *Route-to-Market Validation (Discovery Stage)*
** Worked with Product and Engineering to map all possible routes to launch Bolt Chauffeur in Miami.
** *Outcome:* from an Ops and Product feasibility standpoint, the recommended route was to test with a *third-party dispatch system (*[*LimoAnywhere*|https://www.limoanywhere.com/]*)* to enable bookings without needing the Bolt tech stack.
* *Initial Legal Review*
** Legal ([@armin.allmae|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/UD5NU371C]) has been looped in throughout discovery.
** We’ve had an initial legal review to clarify compliance implications and requirements for each route.
* *Supplier Validation*
** Completed product demos with *LimoAnywhere* to assess capabilities and confirm feasibility for a pilot.
** The platform enables online pre-booked rides, payments, and dispatch via their affiliate network of 50+ Miami fleets.
* *U.S. Ride-Hail Launch Review*
** Revisited the previous ride-hail U.S. assessment.
** A key insight: *insurance cost and risk remain a major blocker* for ride-hail launches. This reinforces why a smaller-scale, fleet-based chauffeur model is an attractive testing ground.

# *What’s Next / In Progress*

* *Input from Extended Functions*
** Policy, Tax, Privacy, Commerce, and Insurance have now joined the channel. We would appreciate your perspectives or early questions as you review the materials shared so far.
* *Legal Document Review (LimoAnywhere) -* [*@armin.allmae*|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/UD5NU371C]*/*[*@iva.buric*|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U036FUPCH5M]
** LimoAnywhere has shared draft contracts (T&Cs, data, and platform agreements).
** We need to confirm whether these can be reviewed *internally* by Legal/Privacy (subject to [MVRA|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/BIZ-252?focusedCommentId=3650585&sourceType=mention] bandwidth) or *via external counsel* as part of the legal questionnaire workstream.
* *Insurance Validation -* [*@daniel.severin*|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U03KA2KSULF]
** We’re testing the *insurance hypothesis* that a private-chauffeur model (working with licensed fleets, not independent drivers) carries _lower risk and cost_ than traditional ride-hailing.
** Early indicators:
*** Chauffeur fleets already maintain *commercial livery insurance* covering passengers, vehicles, and drivers.
*** Bolt’s exposure is therefore *secondary* and can likely be covered under fleet indemnities and platform liability.
*** Lower trip volumes and pre-booked operations further reduce risk relative to on-demand ride-hailing.
** We’ll work with the Insurance team to confirm whether these assumptions hold and what coverage adjustments might be required.

# *Immediate Next Steps*

* *Legal:* confirm who can review the LimoAnywhere legal documentation (internal vs external counsel).
* *Functional input:* each team to review current materials and flag considerations or blockers.
* *Insurance:* provide written feedback on the private-chauffeur risk hypothesis and expected premium implications.
* *Scheduling:* we can arrange a short *cross-functional kickoff next week* to align all functions on objectives, timelines, and open questions.

Hi,

Jorick and I had a conversation, and he walked me through how the changes will look. I’m summarizing everything here for clarity:

We currently have *two indicators* related to job stages in the data:

# *Job stage name* – the detailed stage value coming from GH (e.g., _"Phone Interview"_).
# *Grouped stage* – a broader category that may include multiple job stage names (e.g., _"1st Assessment"_).

OneModel receives the *job stage name* and uses our internal mapping to determine two things:

* Which *grouped stage* it belongs to (e.g., _"Phone Interview"_ → _"1st Assessment"_).
* The *ordering* of stages in OM dashboards.

As I understood from our discussion, you will be harmonizing stage names in GH and do the mapping there to make them more consistent for recruiters. Following this change, we see two possible scenarios:

h3. *Scenario 1*

OM still receives the *detailed job stage names*.
→ In this case, we simply update our mapping to align with your revised naming structure, and OM will continue to show the correct grouped stages and stage order.

h3. *Scenario 2*

OM begins receiving *only grouped stage names*, instead of detailed stage names.
→ In this case, we would need to adjust our transformation process, because it currently expects job stage names to map them into grouped stages.

----

h3. *Action Points*

* *First*, we align on the mapping. I will review your updated mapping and compare it with the current OM version. 
* *Second*, I will raise a discussion with team about potential changes to the transformation script. If needed, we will raise a ticket to OM to get a confirmation.
* *Third*, if possible, it would be very helpful to *test the changes on a limited stage* and track the resulting behavior in the application/scorecards. The, we can confirm how the integration behaves before applying the changes more broadly.

The list is grouped by {{user}} and {{<schema_name.table_name>}}. The included columns are:

* *cluster*. Database cluster
* *hostgroup*. Database cluster ID
* *type*. Database management system [mysql, tidb]
* *collected_at*. Collection [+time.time()+|https://docs.python.org/3/library/time.html#time.time]
* *collected_from.* The PRIMARY database server of the cluster.
* *env*. Environment [prelive, live]
* *user*. Database username
* *table_schema*. The database and table which the user can access, are separated by “.” {{<schema_name.table_name>}}
Where *** means access to all databases and/or all tables.
* *privilege_type*. List of privileges that the user has granted. Between ““, separated by coma.
* *grant_priv*. Does the user have grant privileges {{[Y/N]}}, Having GRANT privilege means it can give PRIVILEGES to other users, and themselves.
* *locked*. Is the user locked {{[Y/N]}} a Locked user cannot establish a connection to the databases.
* *created_at*. Created date for users created by configless.

h3. General Update:

People Partners are done with the review, now cross analysis in progress to check if we are already compliant or have any gaps on our existing job ads. Confluence documentation is in progress.

h3. *People Tech - Recruitment Tools Audit*

The compliance audit reviewed the recruitment process across GEM, Greenhouse, GoodTime, and BrightHire, focusing on data privacy, consent, DEI, access control, auditability, data retention, and vendor compliance. The audit mapped the recruitment workflow end-to-end and evaluated compliance checkpoints in each tool and process stage.

Several areas were found compliant (✔), including candidate data legitimacy in GEM, various Greenhouse compliance elements (consent, accessibility, EEO storage, offer documentation, HRIS integration), Okta-based authentication for most tools, and vendor GDPR commitments.

Multiple areas were flagged as partially compliant (⚠️), including: GEM consent and opt-out mechanisms, DEI segmentation review, Greenhouse data minimization, several GoodTime access and fairness controls, BrightHire transparency, candidate data final retention, tool data flow documentation, and offboarding for tools not integrated with Okta.

One area was marked as non-compliant (❌): no formal quarterly user access review exists across tools.

Additional risk areas and red-flag behaviors were identified for each tool, highlighting issues such as inconsistent consent in sourcing tools, incomplete interview documentation, missing audit trails, manual data retention, unlogged scheduling actions, data exposure risks, and inconsistent use of interview recording workflows.

[https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nZh9TaPDMUZx6Vf76nznP7TSsYkI9VMnsc0rqMbvLPE/edit?tab=t.0|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nZh9TaPDMUZx6Vf76nznP7TSsYkI9VMnsc0rqMbvLPE/edit?tab=t.0|smart-link] 

h3. *Action Points* 

h3. *General / Cross-Tool*

* Document the full data flow between GEM, Greenhouse, GoodTime, and BrightHire (⚠️).
* Establish a formal quarterly user access review process (❌).
* Improve offboarding processes for tools without Okta sign-in (⚠️).
* Periodically review vendor subprocessor lists (currently only done at contract signing).
* Centralize storage of consent forms, reports, and audit results.
* Ensure audit logs are retained and reviewable.
* Ensure compliance findings are reported to HR leadership.
* Schedule regular (quarterly or annual) compliance reviews.
* Assess compliance implications before new tool features or integrations go live.
* Ensure all recruiters receive privacy and tool-compliance training.

h3. *GEM – Sourcing & Outreach*

* Implement/verify consent tracking for outreach (⚠️).
* Add or confirm clear opt-out mechanisms in outreach emails (⚠️).
* Review outreach segmentation for fairness/bias (⚠️).
* Assess automatic data retention processes (no result indicated in the table).
* Document data sourcing methods & legitimacy.
* Ensure opt-outs and engagement sync correctly to ATS.

h3. *Greenhouse – Application, Offer, Closing*

* Review data minimization in application forms (⚠️).
* Implement structured interview kits and required feedback fields.
* Audit and adjust user permissions (admin rights, recruiter visibility).
* Implement automatic candidate data deletion after retention periods.
* Enforce logging of all communications and feedback directly in Greenhouse.
* Ensure final candidate data retention processes meet policy (⚠️).

h3. *GoodTime – Interview Coordination*

* Ensure candidate data is shared securely with interviewers (⚠️).

MDE- 10%

Experiment duration - 11 weeks

Experiment start - 15.12.2025



*Why we use 10% MDE (instead of 2%)?*

* A 10% uplift represents a meaningful business impact, while a 2% uplift is too small to justify the complexity of location-based targeting.
* With a baseline conversion of 6.71% and an average scooter ride price of €1.74, the incremental revenue per 100,000 pushed tourists is:
** 2% uplift: +130 rides → €226 per market → €5,876 across 26 markets
** 10% uplift: +670 rides → €1,165 per market → €30,290 across 26 markets
* A 2% effect (~€6k globally) is within natural market noise and not impactful enough to influence strategy.
* A 10% uplift (~€30k globally) is a material, measurable gain that justifies the targeting logic and experiment investment.

Therefore, the experiment is powered for a 10% MDE, which balances business relevance and feasible experiment duration (~11 weeks).

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The issue has now been resolved. But we still need to adjust the customer’s balance manually.
Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

Currently we are using implementation of {{@bolteu/react-native-haptic-feedback}} from React Native Platform.

That library uses haptics from directly {{expo}}.

We have 4 different haptic types:

* Light
** A feedback type for light feedback
** iOS and Android only
** Used in:
*** {{BugButtonOverlay}} - when pressing bug button
*** {{CollapsibleCounter}} - when pressing on add
*** {{Counter}} - when pressing on add or remove
*** {{LikeProviderButton}} - when pressing on a button
*** {{SelectedFilters}} - when removing selected filter
*** {{RowToggle}} - when pressing on toggle
*** {{BugReporterDrawScreen}} - when saving or clearing drawing
*** {{DevMenuLiveActivityScreen}} - when starting or ending activity
*** {{DevMenuTabAnimationsScreen}} - when resetting tracking
*** {{IconButton}} - when pressing on button
*** {{ScheduleOrderPicker}} - when scrolling date or time
* Medium
** A feedback type for medium feedback
** iOS and Android only
** Used in:
*** {{CollapsibleCounter}} - when pressing on remove
*** {{EmptyProviderSearchState}} - when pressing on Browse Bolt Food button
*** {{Filters}} - when applying filters
*** {{FiltersContextProvider}} - when clearing filters inside of the context
*** {{useQuickFilterController}} - when applying or resetting filters
*** {{ScheduleOrderPicker}} - when updating user selection
*** {{Star}} - when pressing on component
*** {{Thumb}} - when pressing on component
*** {{DishBasketItemContext}} - when updating or removing item from basket
*** {{DeleteAccountResult}} - when submitting account deletion
*** {{SettingsScreen}} - when pressing on log out button
* Success
** A feedback type indicating that a task was successful
** iOS only
** Used in:
*** {{profileVerificationConfirmThunk}} - when {{getDeliveryUserApiClient}} request succeeded
*** {{AddPaymentScreen}} - when new payment method was successfully added
* Failure
** A feedback type indicating that a task has failed
** iOS only
** Used in:
*** {{DishBasketItemContextProvider}} - when pressing on invalid, disabled element in the context

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Hey team [~accountid:712020:853cbe25-4d18-40c3-8211-69c3936bf72f] , I’ve been looped into this ticket by [~accountid:712020:f63df97f-cad1-4718-9bb1-80038488d7e2] to support from privacy side. What I’m interested in is how the ads themselves will look like and what data we’ll exchange. This will help me choose the right approach regarding privacy clauses in the agreement. Please let me know if my below understanding is correct 🙂 🙏 

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*1. What the marketing setup means from a privacy standpoint*
{panel}

Based on the description, the campaign relies on Bolt identifying users who:

* have a Luminor-issued payment card added to their Bolt Food account, or
* have such a card but have not transacted recently.

This targeting is fully performed within Bolt’s environment. We do _not_ share personal data (e.g., card BINs linked to specific users, purchase history, targeting logic, or engagement data) with Luminor.

This distinction is important for two reasons:

* *Risk perspective* - the privacy risk increases significantly only when signals _about users_ are shared externally. In this case, targeting happens entirely on Bolt’s side, using data already processed under our existing privacy notices.
* *User impact* - users simply see a promotional banner in-app. This is a low-intrusion form of marketing and does not materially change how their data is used or who accesses it.

Given this setup, the activity falls under Bolt’s existing transparency and legal bases (contract + legitimate interest for in-app personalised offers). Consent is not required for in-app banners.

FYI adding [~accountid:712020:eb9cd4dd-46ca-47c8-a985-9f940495724a] and [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d]  (Tat - we discussed this agreement and I am covering it as it also relates to rides).

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*2. Does this amount to “personal data collection” between the Parties?*
{panel}

No. Luminor does not receive any personal data from Bolt, nor do they instruct us on how to process data. They only receive aggregated redemption reporting _after_ discounts are used (no user-level data). Bolt remains fully in control of the targeting.

Therefore the *light touch privacy clause in the template is appropriate*, and we keep the statement that the agreement does not require personal data sharing between the Parties. If at any point Luminor expects user-level insights or wants to onboard their own audience, we will need to reassess.

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
*Assessment of overall privacy risk*
{panel}

*Risk level - low.*

* The marketing activity is internal to Bolt.
* No personal data leaves Bolt.
* No requirement for consent under ePrivacy because this is in-app display, not email/SMS/push.
* Transparency is already covered through our Driver/Rider/Food privacy notices.

The picture is a bit more complex regarding giving fleet drivers priority access to pre-booked airport orders. Although this is something we could do, we need to be extra careful with this in the UK as drivers are a lot more sensitive to issues relating to trip allocation (we were subject to a investigation from the UK regulator this year which touched on how Bolt allocates trips to drivers). In practical terms, this means that *we could go ahead with this in the UK* +*_provided that_*+ *we do the following*:

# *Ensure that there is a real and justifiable business need for this* (rather than it just being a ‘nice to have’).
# *Flag somewhere in driver-facing materials* (e.g., in a blog post / FAQ article dealing with M&G): (i) that fleet drivers will be given priority access to pre-booked airport orders; (ii) why this is the case (i.e., why it is important for us to take this approach, such as to ensure the reliability of time-sensitive trips); and (iii) that this would still allow private drivers to accept these orders (albeit further down in the queue). I would be happy to assist with the drafting of this when the time comes - just let me know.
## NB. This is important as one of the main complaints we are seeing from drivers in the UK concerns transparency around topics such as trip allocation. By including the above in something openly available to drivers, we can pre-empt these complaints and lower the risk of any regulatory interest into this feature.
# *Ensure that the priority allocation system has clear lines of accountability*. In other words, we should ensure that: (i) the datapoints / process / algorithm are clearly documented (in case we are ever asked about it and need to provide that the system is robust and proportionate); (ii) the system is designed in such a way as to minimise errors; and (iii) if a driver ever accuses the system of being unfair or broken, we have a way of reviewing the system and addressing any issues as needed.

Happy to discuss if you have any questions 🙂 If you get any updates from the Product team on priority allocation, please be sure to keep the Privacy Team in the loop so that we can review and consider.

+*UPDATE (08.12)*+

*Legal basis / supporting documentation*:

* UK pension regulator has formally informed Bolt that it considers UK drivers to fall within the definition of “workers” (and Bolt as an “employer”) for automatic enrolment purposes.
** Underlying statutory duties for employers re automatic enrolment are under Pt 1 of the [Pension Act 2008|https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2008/30/part/1] (see section 3), which requires UK employers to automatically enrol “_eligible jobholders_” into a qualifying pension scheme.
** Bolt does not agree with this decision. Currently, we are engaging with the pension regulator on a “without prejudice” basis (i.e., Bolt plans to launch the automatic enrolment scheme, but is still arguing that it is not an employer.
* *Importance*: It sounds like we should +*not*+ rely on legal obligations as the legal basis here, as this would be conceding that we are an ‘employer’. As a result, we need to consider either CN, or LI, or consent.
** Ultimately, since the [T&Cs|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OmWqQ9IIdayn-BAjAKH1B8CQYIP7q0hw/edit] state that the pension was (previously) optional, CN is unlikely to apply. legitimate interest seems like it will be the obvious / most practical choice (as it seems the business wants to proceed on an opt-out basis). As such, we should conduct a *legitimate interest assessment* (and a *DPIA* for good measure) ⚠️ 
** Section 7 of the Pensions Act contains a right to opt-out anyway (according to [Iva|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09KXK4DV60/p1765195191241309?thread_ts=1762188941.452099&cid=C09KXK4DV60], the statutory opt-out period is 30 days). We should ensure that *opt-out mechanism* is clear and prevents data sharing ⚠️ 

*Transparency*:

* Since pensions are not covered in the driver privacy notice, best option overall would be *in-time notices* (i.e., disclaimer language in whatever comms we will be sending, informing drivers that their data will be shared) ⚠️  We can consider PN updates in the long term.
** Should include an overview of purpose, legal basis, categories of personal data, and data recipient. Should otherwise include a link to the privacy notice.

*Data Sharing*:

* Zellis:
** *Agreement needs to be amended* (although this is lower risk than Aviva) ⚠️
*** +Subprocessors+: We should ensure more of a shift to specific, rather than general, authorisation.
*** +Audits+: The agreement needs to contain an obligation on Zellis to allow for and contribute to audits (this is legally mandatory).
*** +Costs+: The agreement currently states that DSSR/A32-36 assistance is at Bolt’s expense. We cannot accept this, as they are legally mandatory.
*** +Notification Deadlines+: The agreement does not contain specific deadlines for Zellis to inform Bolt about DSRRs/PDBs.
*** +Indemnities / Liability+: As advised by Legal already, we need a pro-Bolt privacy indemnity and a higher liability cap for Zellis.
** NB. InfoSec has confirmed that Zellis is fine here: [+ISS-1043+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/17/ISS-1043].
* Aviva:
** Only agreements we have with Aviva are [here|https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lNOg_N194uQwEgRieEmx_glmknsfHbJp/view] and [here|https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YZlE04MW2U6Aau5XWTDO7jeJn748gT-m/view]. These were signed when we launched the opt-in pension scheme, and we have not received any others (see [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09KXK4DV60/p1765195191241309?thread_ts=1762188941.452099&cid=C09KXK4DV60]).
*** Clause 7 of the [Corporate Platform Terms of Use|https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lNOg_N194uQwEgRieEmx_glmknsfHbJp/view] deals with data protection. 
**** Parties act as independent controllers. Fine.
**** Parties are required to comply with data protection obligations, notify/cooperate with each other re PDBs, cooperate re regulatory investigations, and document audits. Fine.
**** UK Addendum is incorporated for restricted transfers. Fine.
**** Aviva’s liability for DP violations is capped at £5,000,000. Fine.
**** No obvious pro-Bolt indemnity. However, it looks like there are some hooks to hang Aviva on here, so this is acceptable.
**** Annex 1 (details of processing) and Annex 2 (UK Addendum) seems to be based on Bolt templates. Fine.
***** NB. Data being transferred and processed is driver name, contact details, address, DOB, IP address, transaction history, National Insurance Number, gender and marital status.
*** The other agreement is with drivers, so is not our concern here.
** Iva has confirmed that Aviva will likely want a new agreement for the auto-enrolment setup (see [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09KXK4DV60/p1765268666935239?thread_ts=1762188941.452099&cid=C09KXK4DV60]), which will be heavily based on the previous version. As such, this should be ok - No urgent need to negotiate a new DSA with Aviva ✅

** We should include in-time notices.

However, performing this clean-up only on a quarterly basis would still mean the data remains in Greenhouse longer than allowed, which would put us at risk of GDPR non-compliance. Because of this, raising a ticket every quarter is not an option.

Greenhouse has also informed us that they cannot automate this process on their side because the data belongs to us, and therefore any anonymization actions must be initiated by Bolt. Since notifications are already being sent by email about the anonymization need, we also cannot automate the process internally through Greenhouse.

This leaves us dependent on manual interventions, which increases the likelihood of delays or missed deadlines. We therefore need to identify a more automated or reliably recurring process that ensures all candidate data is anonymized within the required GDPR timelines without relying on tickets or manual triggers.

Hi [~accountid:6233300873c8ec00699dc8b6] , thanks for raising this. This is a global feature, referred to here: [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02CUF8CFCZ/p1763988822063919|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02CUF8CFCZ/p1763988822063919|smart-link] 

Its' aim is not to allow or disallow the use of CCTVs for any kind of drivers (fleet, private), but rather to collect factual information about which drivers have CCTVs installed.

As stated in this [Global guidance, |https://bolt.eu/en/support/articles/21163/] we are not in a position to allow or ban the use of CCTVs, as drivers/fleets have full control over how they collect, and use personal data, including installing and using CCTVs. As they act as “independent data controllers” (i.e. they are fully responsible with compliance with privacy laws), we advise the drivers/fleets to ensure that when they install CCTVs, they comply with law.

This feature (driver logging the presence of CCTV) will later be used to inform passengers about presence of CCTVs in cars. 

In short, this feature (the banner you circled) does not intent to compel drivers to install cameras. What it intends to do is collect information on camera use from those drivers who have it (which again, is outside of our control).

Hi [~accountid:712020:c4b40874-5082-43e8-bf03-940002fefe16] , thanks for flagging this. This is occurring as a result of the reseller model. For VAT purposes only, Bolt Poslovne (B4B entity) is deemed to buy in passenger transport from fleets, and resell it to B4B users (at the same trip price). The purpose of this is purely a customer service - it enables B4B users to receive a single VAT invoice from Bolt instead numerous invoices from a multitude of fleets, reducing administrative burden for the B4B user. For legal purposes, Bolt remains an agent.

Because Bolt is deemed to be inserted into the supply chain, and because it is a VAT-registered, taxable person, all of the resale supplies are then taxable supplies, even if the buy-in was exempt because the driver is below the annual turnover threshold for registration. 

From the perspective of the B4B user, it really shouldn’t matter if it is also a registered, VAT-payer because it will be able to reclaim the added 25% VAT against its taxable output. In the event the B4B user is not a taxable person, the VAT would indeed be an out-of-pocket cost. 

From what I understand, recently the intermediary model was removed from the market. The intermediary model would enable trips provided by non-VAT payers to be exempt when provided to B4B users, but the B4B users would not receive a single VAT invoice. In this model, Bolt is not deemed to be inserted into the supply chain, but rather is an intermediary, agent. 

*In sum, currently it would have no effect to create business categories that include only VAT-payer drivers, effectively separating them from non-VAT drivers for business-related purposes because all rides sold to B4B users in Croatia rely are distributed by Bolt via the reseller model.* 

One thing to consider, which will require time and budget to assess and design if there is sufficient business reason, is to treat the Poslovne entity as a travel agent / tour operator for VAT purposes. This would “turn off” Poslovne’s ability to deduct VAT on input supplies, so it wouldn’t matter whether the fleet is registered or not, from that perspective. Additionally, typically there is no VAT charged on the resale supply to the B4B users. Rather, Bolt would owe output VAT on its margin. In other words, rather than earn a commission, it would buy in the supply at, e.g., Trip Price - Commission = Discounted Rate and resell at the regular Trip Price. Trip Price - Discounted Rate = Margin

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

*App-less Rental (web app for micromobility) for New Riders*
Hi team! I'm happy to share about a functionality designed to make getting on a Bolt ride easier than ever, especially for *users* in the *markets* where we are only *entering*, or for *tourists* that are not familiar with Bolt.*Problem*
In markets, where Bolt is new, or we have high tourist volumes, new riders hesitate when they’re asked to *download* the app before their first trip. This added friction leads to drop-off, especially among tourists and occasional users who simply want a fast, lightweight access to a scooter, or e-bike.*Solution*
To reduce this barrier, we’ve built *App-less Rental,* a streamlined web experience that allows riders to start a trip instantly:

# Riders just scan the QR code on the vehicle.
# They land on a web page where they register and start riding right away.
# The web experience supports up to 3 rides, after which users are encouraged to download the full Bolt app.
# Apple Pay and Google Pay are supported for quick, secure checkout.

*Early Results*
Piloted in *Tallinn* and *Barcelona* since early November:

* *0.24%* of total rides already come from the web experience.
* *26%* of web users convert to the Bolt app.

*Next steps*
We’ll continue piloting in selected markets and explore opportunities for further rollouts based on performance and local market needs.Thanks team for bringing this feature to our *new* users

Regarding the VAT question, I think that:

* The restaurant acts as the seller of the goods (meals/products) and is responsible for issuing an invoice to the final consumer (the customer placing the order via the Bolt Food platform) for each order. This invoice must include the applicable IVA (VAT) in accordance with the general VAT rules applicable to food service operations in Portugal.
* Bolt Food operates as an intermediary platform and not as the buyer of the goods. The restaurant receives payments from Bolt Food on behalf of the final customers, minus the platform commission. As such, the restaurant must:
*# Issue an invoice to the final customer for each sale, including the full amount (with VAT) paid by the customer via the platform.
*# Pay VAT on that amount as it would for any direct sale, in accordance with its normal VAT obligations.
*# Additionally, Bolt Food issues a commission invoice to the restaurant, with the applicable VAT, which the restaurant may deduct according to the general rules.
